title: Laser Power Explained: 5W vs 10W vs 20W vs 48W
metaDescription: What laser wattage actually changes on a diode engraver: speed, cutting depth and price. Four models compared, from the 5W LONGER RAY5 to the 48W ATOMSTACK A40 Pro V2.
author: ByteBuy Team

sections.content: Laser wattage is the headline number on every engraver, and also the most misunderstood. More watts means more energy at the workpiece, which usually means faster engraving, fewer passes when cutting and the ability to handle thicker material. It does not mean sharper detail, and it does not make a machine safer or easier. Here are four catalog machines at four power levels, 5W, 10W, 20W and 48W, so you can see what each step costs: from $252.73 to $999.

sections.title: What Each Power Level Gets You

items.label: 5W: LONGER RAY5 ($252.73)
items.value: Engraving and marking, light cutting of thin material; 0.08x0.08 mm spot, 400x400 mm area, WiFi and offline carving

items.label: 10W: ATOMSTACK A10 Pro V2 ($252.73)
items.value: Faster engraving and cutting of thin wood in fewer passes; 0.06x0.08 mm spot, 410x380 mm area

items.label: 20W: ATOMSTACK A20 Pro V2 ($396.20)
items.value: Cutting with a comfortable margin; 0.08x0.1 mm spot, 400x365 mm area

items.label: 48W: ATOMSTACK A40 Pro V2 ($999)
items.value: Thick material in one pass; listing states 25 mm paulownia or 9 mm MDF, with auto air assist and 500 mm/s

pros: Higher power cuts faster and in fewer passes, which also means less charring on the edge
The jump from 5W to 10W costs nothing in this catalog: the A10 Pro V2 and RAY5 5W are the same price at $252.73, so 10W is the better buy if you do not need the RAY5's WiFi and touch screen
20W is the practical sweet spot for hobby cutting, at $396.20
48W is the only level here whose listing states a one-pass cut in thick wood (25 mm paulownia)
Lower power means a smaller spot on several models, so detail work does not need a high-wattage machine
cons: Watts are not comparable across brands: an advertised figure may be electrical input or optical output, so judge by stated cutting results
The 20W and 48W listings give a larger spot (0.08x0.1 mm) than the 10W (0.06x0.08 mm), so fine detail can be slightly softer
The 48W machine costs $999 and needs stricter safety: enclosure or ventilation, eye protection and constant supervision
More power burns through material faster, which means a bigger fire risk if you are not watching
Stated cutting depths are best cases and vary with material, density and passes

items.question: How many watts do I need to engrave?
items.answer: Engraving needs less power than cutting, and 5W to 10W is enough for wood, leather and painted surfaces. Extra power mainly makes engraving faster.

items.question: How many watts do I need to cut?
items.answer: It depends on the material and thickness. As a rule, double the power halves the number of passes. For thin plywood, 10W works with a few passes, while 20W or more is more comfortable. Check the stated results in the listing.

items.question: Is a 48W diode laser four times better than a 10W?
items.answer: It is much more capable at cutting, but not better at everything. It costs about four times as much and lists the same bed class, so choose it only if you cut thick material regularly.

items.question: Why is the 5W RAY5 the same price as the 10W ATOMSTACK?
items.answer: They are different brands and feature sets. The RAY5 5W lists WiFi, a touch screen and offline carving, while the A10 Pro V2 lists higher power and a finer spot. Pick the feature set you value.

items.question: What about 40W machines?
items.answer: The catalog's 40W option is the Creality Falcon T1, a much more expensive 5-in-1 machine, so it is outside this price range. See our Falcon guide for details.

sections.content: Choose power for the cutting you plan to do, not for the number on the box. For engraving, 5W to 10W is plenty. For regular cutting, 20W is the sweet spot. Go to 48W only when thick material in one pass is the job, and budget for the safety equipment that comes with it.
